slots.label: absolute-time misconception
slots.description: There is one universal time and one universal simultaneity that all observers must agree on.
slots.repair: Special relativity rejects absolute simultaneity for distant events; different inertial frames can assign different times consistently.
slots.repairQuestion: Can two distant events be simultaneous in one inertial frame but not in another?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner says yes, simultaneity of distant events can differ by frame.

slots.label: visual-delay misconception
slots.description: Time dilation is only an illusion caused by signal travel time or looking at moving clocks.
slots.repair: Light travel delay is separate from the relativistic coordinate effect; after correcting observations, inertial frames still compute time dilation.
slots.repairQuestion: If observers correct for light-travel time, does special-relativistic time dilation disappear?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner says no, time dilation remains as a frame-dependent measurement, not mere viewing delay.

slots.label: one-sided moving-clock misconception
slots.description: Only one spaceship is really moving, so only its clock really slows in all frames.
slots.repair: In inertial relative motion, each frame may treat itself as at rest and the other as moving; resolving reunion comparisons requires the full path and often acceleration or frame changes.
slots.repairQuestion: During constant relative motion, can each inertial observer consistently describe the other ship as moving?
slots.repairCriteria: Repaired when the learner says yes, motion is relative between inertial frames and each can use its own frame consistently.

Special relativity says the laws of physics and the speed of light are the same in inertial frames. As a result, elapsed time and simultaneity are frame-dependent: moving clocks are time-dilated for defined event pairs, and distant simultaneity is not absolute. These effects are not illusions, broken clocks, or simple visual-delay artifacts.
